lesson_title: The Boulder Stacks That Were Built Underground
hook_text: Those balanced boulders on granite koppies? They were rounded off underground — before anyone could see them.
clip_script: You have seen them from the road: round granite boulders stacked three and four high on a koppie, like giants played a game and walked away. Here is the trick — the giants were underground. Stack sugar cubes into a block and let tea seep along every gap. Each cube gets attacked from the outside in, but not evenly: a corner is hit from three directions at once, an edge from two, a flat face from only one. Corners melt first. Every cube rounds itself into a ball. Granite does exactly this below the surface. The rock is already cracked into blocks by natural joints; groundwater creeps along those cracks for tens of thousands of years, rotting the rock inward from every side; and each buried block rounds into a hard corestone sitting in its own crumbly rot, like a marble in wet sand. Then comes the unveiling. Rain and rivers strip away the soft rot, and the survivors are left standing — still stacked exactly where the joints put them, but now balanced in the open air. That is a tor. Nobody piled it up. It was revealed. And the same granite tells a second story next door: where the cracks were far apart, the rock could only peel in curved onion shells and polish itself into a bald shining dome — that is Paarl Mountain. One rock, two magic tricks, both performed in the dark.
visual_style: Sugar cubes dissolving corner-first in tea morphing into an underground cutaway of corestones rounding in red grus, then the soil peeling away to leave a real stacked tor, closing on a rain-slicked granite dome.
mood: Reveal-the-secret wonder, like a magic trick explained.
pacing: Playful open on the boulders, methodical middle through the sugar-cube mechanism, fast satisfying unveiling at the end.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never see a pile of balanced boulders as an accident again.
